name: Treaty at Camp Union, near the Yuba River (1851), unratified California treaty F
aka: Treaty F of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 3 set apart 'forever' for the sole use and occupancy of the ten tribes a district from the Bear river at the western line of Camp Far West, twelve miles up the Bear, due north to the Yuba river, twelve miles down the Yuba and south to the start.

Brood mares, milch cows, work cattle, mules, ploughs, hoes, spades and grindstones; a farmer with two assistants, a carpenter, a wheelwright, a blacksmith and school teachers, paid by the United States for five years and as long after as the President thought advisable (Kappler, vol. 4, as excerpted by Oklahoma State University).

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty F in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.what: The Nisenan state that their leaders signed the Camp Union Treaty in good faith, that the United States never fulfilled its obligations under it, and that the Senate, pressed by California's new government, declined in secret to ratify it, leaving Nisenan land open to settlers and miners.

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 287, 288 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

plain.promised: A district between the Bear and Yuba rivers set apart forever for ten tribes, plus livestock, ploughs, tools, a farmer, a carpenter, a wheelwright, a blacksmith and school teachers paid by the United States for five years.
plain.happened: The Senate refused to ratify the treaty on July 8, 1852, and kept it secret until 1905. The Nisenan say this left their land open to settlers and miners.
plain.today: The treaty remains unratified. A 1928 Act let California Indians sue for the promised lands and compensation; the amount finally paid has not been traced.

nationVoice.nation: Nevada City Rancheria Nisenan Tribe (through its nonprofit HUṠWEJ, formerly CHIRP)
nationVoice.summary: The Nisenan history says Nisenan leaders signed the Camp Union Treaty in 1851 in good faith, as a last attempt to protect their people and homelands amid gold rush violence, that the United States never met its obligations because the Senate secretly declined to ratify it under pressure from California, and that without legal protection Nisenan land kept being overrun.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: none.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

In Article 3 the signing tribes gave up their claims to other lands; because the Senate rejected the treaty, the United States took the land without the reserved tract or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).

Audit 2026-11-08: promises corrected against treaty F as printed in Heizer (1972), the treaty text at https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/83366/files/arfs003-001.pdf; Heizer omits some of this treaty's articles, so the goods and staff are taken from Oklahoma State University's excerpt of Kappler vol. 4 (https://oms.library.okstate.edu/s/oklahoma-built/item/21830), and any subsistence (beef and flour) article was not checked; the earlier 'beef and flour during 1851 and 1852' line was removed because it was copied from the other treaties.
